entry.title: Working together with Grok Bot in a Claude Code session, enabled by Dozable
entry.summary: Claude Code superpowers granted to your Grok Bots.
entry.content:
I quickly fell for Grok Bot's charm and capabilities. From marketing to product management (I even have a librarian), they are all performing their daily duties and I have come to rely on them. However, they can't design and they can't code, at least not to the same level as Claude Code. I didn't want to give up either. I wanted Grok Bot keeping everything on track, and Claude Code doing the hard design and coding. So the next step felt obvious: let Grok Bot hand that work to Claude Code and get on with it by itself, while I kept an eye on everything.

The goal was to give each of my Grok Bots its own Claude Code workspaces on my own Macs, so the bots and the people on my team can work together in them. The bots do the delegated work in their sessions. A person keeps full visibility of every session, and can watch one or jump in and type whenever they need to.

I run Grok Bots with company roles. One of them, Cheto, is my CTO bot. A bot's workspaces are long-lived Claude Code sessions on a Mac, one per workstream. For this to work, the bot has to be able to hand work to its own sessions and read the answers, without ever taking a session away from the person at the keyboard.

That turned out to be two separate problems: how a bot gets a message into a session that is already running, and how the reply gets back out. This post covers what I tried, what worked, and the part that still doesn't.

The pictures in this post are frames of an interactive diagram of the setup. A public page for the interactive version is not up yet, so the post uses the stills only.

The problem#

The obvious approach failed first. On the Claude Code version I had (2.1.321), there was no claude send command. Resuming a running background session with --resume and extra flags didn't continue it. It started a copy with a new ID. So "stop the session, resume it with the next instruction" was the only way to deliver a message, and that is clumsy. It also put the session's context at risk every time.

Permissions caused the second problem. I ran my delegated sessions with permission prompts skipped. When a sender that wasn't in that mode messaged one of those sessions, Claude Code held the message on a Deny / Deliver prompt. In a background session with no terminal attached, nobody sees that prompt. In my probe it was still waiting about four minutes later. That explained a run of approval requests I had been seeing.

There's a third, quieter problem. A background session that asks a question has no terminal to ask it in, so it sits there, blocked.

What worked#

The fix was to stop treating the bot as a direct sender and give it a mailbox instead.

The mailbox is another Claude Code session. It's long-lived, it runs in the background, and it starts from a scratch directory rather than a work repo. Its only job is to send messages to work sessions and print what comes back.

Sending uses Claude Code's own cross-session messaging. Inside the mailbox, Claude uses its built-in SendMessage tool to reach a work session. I address the target by its exact session name. In my probe, the short IDs that claude agents prints didn't match as addresses, and names stayed stable when processes were respawned. A reply arrives in the mailbox labelled Message from @<sender-name>. Claude Code's cross-session messaging docs describe the same tools, ListAgents and SendMessage, and the same "Message from @name" preview.

The two frames below are from the later diagram, not from the 10 November probe. They show the worker typing the instruction into the relay, then the relay sending by exact name.

Matching permission modes avoids the held-message prompt. With both ends skipping permission prompts, messages were delivered with no approval prompt. The docs describe the default rule: a session that bypasses prompts holds messages from a session that doesn't. A receiver started with crossSessionInbound set to accept admitted a non-bypass sender in my probe. I haven't applied that setting to a real work session.

Skipping permission prompts is a trade-off, not a recipe. With prompts off, a session acts without asking. I accepted that for disposable probe sessions in a scratch directory on a machine I control. For real work, the plan relies on other limits instead: a scoped brief, isolated worktrees, pull-request review, and stopping a session when needed. If those limits aren't in place, don't copy this setting.

Later messages go in by attaching to the mailbox and typing. This was the missing piece. On the evening of 10 November I started a throwaway mailbox and a throwaway receiver, then left both idle. A small expect script ran claude attach on the mailbox and typed one line: SEND R1. The mailbox sent the message, the receiver acknowledged it, and the reply showed up on the attached screen. I then did the same for SEND R2 and SEND R3. Each line went in only after the previous reply had printed. The process IDs didn't change across the three rounds, and nothing was restarted or resumed. From typing a line to seeing the reply took about 29, 15 and 18 seconds.

The human path is separate. A person's way in doesn't go through the bot or the mailbox. Claude Code documents claude attach <session> for opening a background session in a terminal, and detaching leaves the session running. Cheto's path and a person's are designed to meet only at the work session.

The bot reaches the Mac through a Cursor worker. For this workflow, Cheto reaches the Mac through a Cursor agent running there as a My Machines worker. Cursor's docs describe the split: the agent loop runs in Cursor's cloud, and terminal commands and file edits run on your machine over an outbound connection. That worker runs the claude commands. It checks what's running with claude agents --json --all, attaches to the mailbox to type, and reads replies with claude logs when nobody is attached. The plan keeps supervision of real work in GitHub: delegated sessions open draft pull requests, and Cheto reviews those through the GitHub connector instead of pulling transcripts off the Mac.

Why this is interesting#

  • No new plumbing on the Claude side. The mailbox is an ordinary Claude Code session using a built-in tool. I didn't add a server or a custom protocol.
  • A bot and a person each have their own way in. That is what keeps the person's visibility intact: the bot doesn't need the person's terminal, and the person doesn't need the bot to see or type into a session. I haven't tested whether both can use the same session at the same moment.
  • Supervision stays readable. In the plan, the record of real work is a draft pull request checked against acceptance criteria, not a scrape of a terminal.

Limits, plainly#

What I have proved is narrow: repeated exchanges between one mailbox and one receiver, on throwaway sessions, on one Mac and one Claude Code version (2.1.322). The real work session in the diagram wasn't messaged. These things are not proved:

  • Return notifications. Nothing in the tested path wakes an idle Cursor worker or Cheto when a reply arrives. Something still has to attach or poll. A local hook on a separate mailbox did record unsolicited incoming messages to a file, but it notified no one. A webhook routine for a return bridge has been prepared. It isn't connected, it hasn't been live-tested, and it still needs its endpoint and a securely supplied key.
  • Routing to a second work session. A retarget line to a second receiver never became a turn in the mailbox.
  • A human attaching while the mailbox is messaging the same session. Not part of the 10 November probe. The demonstration below is a later account, from a transcript, and it is not a re-run of that probe.
  • The typing script as a bridge. The terminal UI breaks words up on screen, so the script's simple text matching didn't work reliably. It was good enough for a probe and isn't a deployed integration.

Claude Code is also moving quickly. Its current docs describe other routes I haven't tried in this setup: replying from agent view's peek panel, resuming a running session with a prompt, an idle notification option on SendMessage, and channels for pushing events into a session. Some of these may make parts of this setup simpler, or unnecessary. I'll test them before I say so.

So the 10 November probe is a narrow result, not a deployed system. It proved that a bot can hold a repeated exchange with a running session through a mailbox. A human attaching is a separate, documented way in. On that probe, using both on the same session at the same time, and getting a reply back to the bot without polling, were still untested.

Showing it to a new team member#

On Friday 13 November 2026, in Sydney, I showed this setup to a new team member and used it for real. The quotes below come from a call transcript received at 13:04 Australia/Sydney. The transcription may be imperfect. These are lightly edited quotes. They have not yet been checked by the speaker:

"this is really using it for real, right? So this sandbox is running. You can see there's three. So these are three sessions, three Claude sessions."

"see these messages here? ... these are from Grok bot."

"Sending the messages."

"So I can see them. I can jump in and interact. I've got full visibility and it's all kind of packaged in these sandboxes that are templated. So if the bot needs to spin up an environment for Remotion, it can do it really quickly."

How this relates to Dozable#

Dozable is what makes the goal practical: each bot's Claude Code sessions run in templated sandboxes on my Macs, so a bot can have its own workspaces and a person can still see all of them. The same shape is in the setup I use now. Bots send prompts into live Claude Code sessions through Dozable's relay, and the prompts are typed into the session. Dozable holds the terminal, so several clients can attach to one session with doz attach. A person can watch live, and a watcher is not a reason for the bot to stop. If a person types, the bot yields and does not overwrite text it did not write. A Cursor worker handles the repository work. Approvals stay with a person. The setup also names a Remotion sandbox, m3-remotion, on m1max3. The speed in the quote is about a templated Remotion environment. This post is not adding a separate claim about how fast that named sandbox booted.

About Dozable#

Dozable gives each coding agent its own small Linux computer on your Mac, so you can let it work. A sandbox starts in about a third of a second, and your API keys stay on the Mac. Try it at dozable.com.

entry.title: Dozable 0.37 - sessions on this Mac
entry.summary: Dozable 0.37 holds sessions on this Mac for work a Linux sandbox cannot do, and adds Claude Code with local models, your own recipes, and dotfiles in every sandbox.
entry.content:
It's on the stable channel now, as 0.37.46, and includes everything since 0.35.

Sessions on this Mac#

Dozable holds terminal sessions on this Mac, for work a Linux sandbox cannot do: Swift, Xcode, signing and notarisation. A session runs as you: your files, Keychain and network, with no sandbox and no proxy.

The dashboard's This Mac page lists them. Opening a session starts read-only; Type into it switches to typing. Start one with doz run @mac; other devices see none of this by default.

Claude Code with other models#

Claude Code can use a model server on this Mac (Ollama, LM Studio or oMLX), OpenRouter's Anthropic endpoint, or Anthropic as before. The proxy lets that sandbox reach only the port you chose.

Recipes and dotfiles#

You can add your own recipe with doz recipe new or doz recipe add, and a signed community catalogue with doz recipe source add. A sandbox can use your dotfiles from a git repository or a folder on this Mac: fetched on the Mac, applied as the image's user, and never overwriting an existing file.

Also new#

  • Claude Code keeps its conversations, instead of deleting them after 30 days. A cleanup period you already set is left alone.
  • A sandbox's Files tab shows /workspace as a live, editable tree. Open folder opens it in the Finder or an editor on this Mac (doz files open).
  • doz sessions send types into a session from a script; doz sessions screen prints the screen as it is now. Both work on a sandbox's sessions too.
  • Dozable offers Claude Code, Codex, pi and OpenCode (1 and 2), with OpenRouter as the gateway. The other tools, and Vercel AI Gateway, are unpublished for now and return in a later release; sandboxes already made with them keep working.

Fixed#

  • A busy sandbox is no longer starved of memory after a wake, and one unresponsive sandbox can no longer hang doz ls.
  • A sandbox that stopped answering is shown as "not answering".

Upgrade#

0.37 starts fresh: settings, the store and caches live in new doz folders, and nothing is migrated from the earlier paths. The install and upgrade page says what to do before and after. If you are upgrading from 0.35, trust the Homebrew tap once, then upgrade:

Then try a session on this Mac, or Claude Code with a local model.

entry.title: Dozer Sandbox is now Dozable
entry.summary: Dozer Sandbox has a new name, Dozable, in 0.36.1; the doz command, your sandboxes, your settings and how you upgrade all stay as they are.
entry.content:
A search for "dozer sandbox" finds sand toys, toy bulldozers and a sand-play centre in Kansas, and it will for a long time: both are everyday words. Dozable is one word that only means us, and it says what the product does: sandboxes that doze and wake in about a third of a second.

Dozable 0.36.1 is on the stable channel now.

What changes#

  • The name. Dozable, everywhere: the dashboard, doz --help, the manual and this blog.
  • The website moves to dozable.com. Every dozersandbox.com address keeps working and takes you to the same page.
  • The Homebrew tap is now dozable/tap. New installs use it:

What stays#

  • doz, the Dozable command line. Every command and option is the same.
  • Your sandboxes, images and settings. Nothing moves on your Mac.
  • Upgrading. If you installed from dozer-sandbox/tap, you don't need to do anything: that name keeps working, and doz upgrade uses it.
  • Your subscription. You're still subscribed to the same topics, and unsubscribing is still one click.

Upgrade#

entry.title: Dozable 0.35 - doz try, and keys from any provider
entry.summary: Dozable 0.35 adds doz try for any of 42 coding agents and AI tools, keys from any major provider or gateway, a choice of model, and OpenCode 2.
entry.content:
It's on the stable channel now, as 0.35.1. It includes everything from 0.34, which went straight from canary to this release.

doz try#

One command puts you in a throwaway sandbox with any of 42 coding agents and AI tools: its own empty folder, a network that reaches only its model, and your key kept on your Mac. doz try has its own post.

Keys from any provider, and a choice of model#

Use a key from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or xAI, or one key for many models through OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway. Dozable can also read a key from 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager or a command each time it's needed. A try's setup and New Sandbox let you pick the model from the gateway's own list, and doz models lists them.

The Accounts & keys page groups keys by provider, with the tools each one serves. A key that stopped working comes first, with what the provider said and how to fix it.

Tools#

  • OpenCode 2 is the opencode Dozable recommends; OpenCode 1 stays as opencode@1. Its free OpenCode Zen models need no key.
  • Grok Build, Factory Droid and Docker Agent report working and done in the dashboard.

Also new#

  • doz search aider says whether Dozable runs a tool, and how, or why not yet.
  • A sandbox's web page opens in your Mac's browser: the sandbox's Open button, or doz open.

Fixed#

  • Icons in the dashboard no longer blink every few seconds.
  • A key its provider refuses shows as refused, instead of a green "ok".

Upgrade#

entry.title: doz try - any of 42 AI tools in one command
entry.summary: doz try puts you in a throwaway sandbox with a coding agent or AI tool, its own empty folder, a network that reaches only its model and your key kept on your Mac.
entry.content:
Pick a tool and Dozable makes the sandbox, starts it and puts you in it. Nothing is installed on your Mac, and nothing of yours is shared with it. The first try of a tool prepares its image, which takes a few minutes, once.

What a try gets#

  • A new empty folder under your projects folder, shared at /workspace, so what the tool makes is on your Mac. Never one of yours.
  • A network that reaches its model and nothing else. Every other host is refused and logged.
  • Your key, kept on your Mac. The sandbox only ever holds a placeholder. No key yet? The try asks for one, once.

--dry-run shows all of it before anything is made: the version, every host it can reach, the folder and the key.

When you leave, it asks whether to sleep it, delete it or keep it running. Deleting it removes its folder too, and asks first if the tool left files there.

42 tools#

Claude Code, Codex and pi, plus Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Goose, Qwen Code, Cline, OpenHands, Crush and more coding agents. And AI tools such as Fabric, llm, AIChat, ShellGPT, promptfoo and Google Stitch. The manual lists them all, with what each needs.

Choose the model#

Use a key from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or xAI, or one key for many models through OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway. OpenCode can also use OpenCode Zen's free models, with no key at all.

In the dashboard#

Try → Quick try shows the same tools as cards. Search, or filter by kind and category, and Try now opens its setup: where it gets its model, your key and the folder.

Each try opens on its Guide: what the tool is, the facts of this try, and its first commands. Run types a step into the tool's session; Copy puts it on your clipboard.

doz try is in Dozable 0.35. Upgrade with doz upgrade, then doz try.

entry.title: OpenCode 2 is in Dozable
entry.summary: OpenCode 2, a rebuild of the open-source coding agent around one shared background service, now runs in Dozable beside OpenCode 1, on your own key or OpenCode Zen's free models.
entry.content:
OpenCode 2 is out, and you can try it in a sandbox with one command. OpenCode 1 stays available, so a project that depends on it keeps working.

It needs Dozable 0.35, now on the stable channel.

In the dashboard, OpenCode's card in Quick try has a Version choice; it starts on 2. Sandboxes you already have stay on the version they were made with.

What's new in OpenCode 2#

Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, announced 2.0 on 12 October as "a major overhaul" (their post), about three months after its public beta. Its changelog has moved to the 2.x series, so 2 is now OpenCode's main release (The New Stack has a good account of the release).

  • One service, several interfaces. OpenCode now starts a single background service. The terminal interface, the web app and the desktop app all talk to it, so you can start a session in the terminal and continue it in the browser. Your own scripts can find and use the same service.
  • A new API that lets the agent manage itself. The agent can create a git worktree for a new task, move a session into it, or find and interrupt a session that is stuck. Scripts reach the API through @opencode/client; @opencode/sdk embeds OpenCode in your own application (SDK docs).
  • Code Mode. Instead of one tool call per round trip to the model, the agent writes a short JavaScript program that calls several MCP tools or APIs and works with the results, for example reading bug reports from one service and filing issues in another. It is the default for every MCP server.
  • Work in the background. Subagents and shell commands can run while you keep working with the main agent: a code review by a subagent on another model, or a long test run that reports back when it finishes. A shortcut (ctrl+b) moves a running task to the background.
  • Plugins. More than 80 of its own features are now plugins, terminal-interface plugins are stable, and plugins hot-reload, so OpenCode can write a plugin and use it in the same session (how they rebuilt it).

What breaks: plugins written for OpenCode 1 don't load in 2, and integrations built on the old server API need updating.

In Dozable#

OpenCode 2 gets what every tool in Dozable gets:

  • Your key stays on your Mac. Use a key from xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway; the sandbox only ever holds a placeholder. OpenCode Zen's free models take no key at all.
  • A locked network that reaches its model and nothing else, and a folder of its own. OpenCode 2's background service runs inside the sandbox and needs nothing more.
  • A guide beside the try with the first commands to run.
  • Its web app on your Mac: run opencode pair in the sandbox and open the link it prints, or use the sandbox's Open button; it shows in your browser, on this Mac only.

Outside Dozable, OpenCode 1 users move with opencode upgrade --major or /update; since 1.19 it no longer updates itself (1.19.0 release notes). In Dozable you choose the version by name instead, and the sandbox's version comes from Dozable's checked recipe.

Ways to try it#

OpenCode Zen's free models need no account and no key. The picker and doz models --provider opencode-zen show each model's data terms; some may use what you send to improve their models.

Or your own key from xAI, OpenAI or Anthropic, or one key for many models through OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway:

No key for that provider yet? The try asks for one, once, or add it first with doz account add openrouter --provider openrouter. Add --dry-run to any of these to see what it would make and what it can reach, without making anything. In the dashboard, Try → Quick try → OpenCode has the same choices: the Version, and where OpenCode gets its model, with a list of a gateway's models to search.

Why OpenCode 1 stays#

A major version changes what your setup depends on: here, plugins and the API. Dozable pins each tool to a version it has checked. opencode now means OpenCode 2, the version Dozable recommends; OpenCode 1 stays one word away, as opencode@1, and keeps getting 1.x updates. An existing sandbox never moves to a new major version by itself.

New to Dozable? Getting started takes a few minutes.

entry.title: Grok Build now tells Dozable what it's doing
entry.summary: Grok Build 1.0.52 reports when it's working, waiting for you or done, and Dozable 0.35 shows it in the dashboard, as it does for Claude Code and pi.
entry.content:
Grok Build 1.0.52 reports its status, and Dozable 0.35 runs that version. Start a Grok Build sandbox and leave it to work; the dashboard shows when it's busy, when it needs you, and when it's finished.

What you see#

While Grok Build works, its tab says working, and a dot beside the sandbox in the sidebar says something is going on.

When it stops to ask you something, such as permission to run a command, a notice at the top of the dashboard says so, with an Open button that takes you straight to the session, whichever page you're on.

When it finishes, the tab says done. All sessions shows the same on every tile, so with several agents running you can see which one is still busy and which is waiting for you.

Where it comes from#

xAI's changelog for 1.0.52 lists "support for OSC 7501". That's a terminal escape sequence for program status, proposed by Mitchell Hashimoto: a program asks the terminal whether it understands the sequence, and if it does, reports its state each time it changes.

Inside every sandbox, Dozable answers that question for each session and keeps the latest report, whether or not the dashboard is open. Nothing is read from the screen or guessed: Dozable shows exactly what Grok Build reports.

Agents that report their status#

Claude Code, pi and now Grok Build report their status. So do Factory Droid and Docker Agent, which also arrive in 0.35. When another tool adds support, Dozable turns it on in that tool's recipe once we've seen it work.

Upgrade to 0.35, then doz try grok.

entry.title: Introducing Dozable
entry.summary: Fast, resumable, secure Linux sandboxes for AI coding agents on your Mac — free and open source. Here's what it is, why it exists, and how to try it in a minute.
entry.content:
Coding agents are at their best when you stop approving every command. They're at their most worrying then too: the agent can read your files, run anything, and reach any site, all with your keys in its environment.

Dozable gives each agent its own small Linux computer on your Mac, so you can let it work.

What a sandbox is#

Each sandbox is a small Linux virtual machine with one project folder from your Mac inside it, at /workspace. Run Claude Code, Codex or pi in it with the permission prompts off: the VM is the boundary.

  • Fast. A sandbox starts in about a third of a second and pauses in a millisecond.
  • Resumable. Put it to sleep and it gives its memory back. Wake it and every program is still running where you left it, mid-sentence.
  • Secure. The network goes through a policy you can read, and your API keys never go inside: the agent sees a placeholder, and the real key is added on your Mac on the way out.

Try it#

You need a Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 26 or later, and Homebrew.

The dashboard opens on a short setup wizard: it checks your Mac, asks how your agent should sign in, and prepares an image. Then New sandbox and you're in. Prefer the terminal? doz onboard, then doz up in a project folder.

Free and open source#

Dozable is free, and its source is on GitHub.

This blog is where news, early access and tips will appear. They're also sent by email to anyone who signs up for them. Thanks for reading, and for trying it.

entry.title: Dozable 0.33 - see what your agent is doing
entry.summary: Dozable 0.33 shows what each agent is doing at a glance, upgrades with one command, runs the dashboard in the background, and ends setup with an optional sign-up.
entry.content:
It's on the stable channel now, as 0.33.1. Here's each change.

See what the agent is doing#

Claude Code and pi now tell Dozable what they're doing: working, done, waiting for your answer, or stopped by an error. Dozable shows it in the dashboard wherever the session appears, so you can leave an agent to work and glance back when it matters.

While the agent works, its tab shows working, and a dot beside the sandbox in the sidebar says something is going on.

When the agent stops to ask you something, such as permission to run a command, a notice appears at the top of the dashboard saying what it wants, with an Open button that takes you straight to the session. You see it on whichever page you're on.

When it finishes, the tab says done and the notice tells you so. The same status shows on every tile in All sessions, so with several sandboxes running you can see at a glance which agent is still busy and which is waiting for you.

The status shows while the dashboard is open (doz ui). Claude Code needs version 2.1.295 or later, and pi 1.1.0 or later.

How it works#

It uses a terminal escape sequence: bytes mixed into a program's output that the terminal acts on instead of showing, the same way programs set a window's title or colours. This one is OSC 7501, for program status (Mitchell Hashimoto's write-up).

  • The handshake: a program asks the terminal whether it understands the sequence (ESC ] 7501 ; ? ST). If the terminal answers, the program reports its state (working, done, blocked or error, with a short message) each time it changes.
  • Inside the sandbox: every session runs under a small holder process that reads everything the program writes, whether or not anyone is watching. It answers that question, keeps the latest report, and passes the output on unchanged.
  • On your Mac: the Dozable host watches each running session's status, and the dashboard draws it.

Nothing is read from the screen or guessed: Dozable shows exactly what the agent itself reports.

doz upgrade#

One command moves you to the newest version on your channel. It asks first; -y skips the question.

The dashboard in the background#

doz ui --detach runs the dashboard without holding a terminal, and doz ui stop stops it from any terminal.

Staying in touch#

Setup now ends with an optional sign-up for release news, early access, and tips and tricks, by email. Skip it, or sign up later with doz signup.

Fixed in 0.33.1: the agent can write your workspace again#

Since 0.30, an agent in a sandbox could read a shared project folder but not change it, and git refused the folder ("dubious ownership"). 0.33.1 fixes it. After upgrading, a sandbox that was running, asleep or hibernated needs a doz shutdown NAME and then doz start NAME; one that was shut down picks up the fix at its next start.

Upgrade#

New to Dozable? Getting started takes a few minutes.
